William Contreras earned World Series MVP honors after delivering an outstanding performance in the Milwaukee Brewers' five-game triumph over the Tampa Bay Rays. He capped off his impressive series with an RBI double in the decisive Game 5, finishing the matchup with eight hits and four RBIs across five games.
Just days after capturing the World Series championship and MVP honors, Contreras added another distinction to his growing list of accolades, this time earning recognition in a more lighthearted and modest fashion.
"I don't want to offend any of the other catchers in the league," Contreras remarked via an interpreter.
"The last thing I want to do is offend any of them, But sitting up here today, champion of the world, I feel like I'm the best catcher in the league. Again, that's no disrespect to any of them. That's the last thing I want to do. But today I feel like I'm the best catcher in the world."
William Contreras' MVP run with the Brewers
Contreras' playoff run has given him a strong argument for being considered baseball's best catcher. He made a major impact at the plate, batting .373 with three home runs and nine RBIs throughout the postseason.
His contributions were especially noticeable in the World Series, where he recorded multiple hits in three consecutive games to help Milwaukee take a 3-0 series advantage. He was just as effective behind the plate, throwing out four baserunners and winning 10-of-13 ABS challenges while showcasing his pitch-framing skills.
Few catchers can match the impact Contreras made on both offense and defense throughout the postseason. His role in bringing a championship to Milwaukee only strengthens his case as one of the game's premier players at the position. After a performance like that, anyone looking to challenge his claim as baseball's top catcher will have a high bar to clear.

ST. PETERSBURG — The Brewers won by a mile because they're obsessed with the inches.
Nobody would describe the final outcome of Milwaukee's emphatic beatdown on Monday — a 10-1 drubbing of the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 3 of the World Series — as "close." Not since 2015 has there been a larger margin of victory in a World Series game. The Brewers' 16-to-3 hit advantage over the flailing Rays was the third-largest in Fall Classic history. Starter Robert Gasser allowed just one one hit and faced the minimum across six brilliant innings, becoming the first lefty to do that in a World Series game since Sandy Koufax in 1965. A massive gathering of Brewers fans, an estimated 30% of the crowd, was there to witness it all, their voices joyously hoarse by the end.
It was a shellacking of historic proportions.
But Milwaukee's commanding 3-0 series lead, one that places this franchise on the precipice of its first championship, was earned in the margins on a bang-bang play that folks in the Badger State will remember for a long time.
Up a pair in the top of the fifth, the Brewers put runners on first and second against Tampa Bay starter Freddy Peralta. Milwaukee catcher William Contreras, the best hitter in these playoffs, ripped a two-hopper toward third baseman Junior Caminero. In a spinning motion, Tampa's talented talisman snagged the pearl and flicked it to second baseman Ben Williamson as a full-bore Christian Yelich slid into the bag. Umpire Dan Bellino punched his fist. The FOX graphic evaporated from the screen. Multiple members of Tampa Bay's between-innings hype squad jogged onto the outfield track for some type of giveaway.
Yelich, though, clung to the bag with his left hand as he motioned adamantly toward Belino with his right.
"Safe, safe."
Safe, indeed.
The Brewers challenged the call. Before Bellino could finish announcing the overturn, Tampa Bay skipper Kevin Cash was already headed toward the mound to pull Peralta.
But no move, at that point, could have stopped the inevitable.
"The whole game was changed when Yeli was safe at second," Brewer manager Pat Murphy insisted afterwards. "That's just a hustle play. When your leader makes that play, that says it all. The game was changed because he did a little thing that anybody can do."
Yelich, by beating the throw to second, turned a dead frame into the inning of a lifetime. The floodgates soon burst, sweeping away Tampa's next pitcher, Cam Booser. On a 2-2 count, he served a mid-zone fastball to second baseman Brice Turang, who scorched one off shortstop Taylor Walls' glove and into the outfield. Milwaukee's lead was doubled.
As the sizable traveling contingent — a bar down the street sold out of Miller Lite before first pitch — went berzerk, the Fox broadcast panned to a young Rays fan, who could be seen uttering to his companion a harsh and humbling realization: "That's the series."
Milwaukee, though, would leave no doubt. And then some.
Their next five batters all found grass, with each consequential hit eliciting louder and louder roars from the armada of traveling Wisconsinites. In total, the Brewers strung together seven consecutive two-out hits to plate eight two-out runs, a World Series record. It was an all-time heater and a fitting performance from a pridefully selfless Brewers offense that has prioritized passing the baton over hitting big flies all season long.
"Nobody wants to be the hero," hitting coach Dan Vogelbach boasted.
That might be true, but Yelich, with his mad dash to second, was the under-the-radar hero of this evening.
With the right-handed Contreras at the plate and a runner on second, Rays first baseman Ryan Villade was shaded toward second, opting not to hold Yelich on. That allowed the Brewers' captain to take a much larger-than-average lead off first base. By the time Contreras swung, Yelich was already about 30 feet from the bag, his right foot in the air ready to break in either direction. As the ball bounced toward Caminero, Yelich landed and broke hard for second.
"You have to understand where you're at in space," Yelich explained postgame. "You're lengthening your primary [lead] in case there's a ball in the hole or some sort of play happens where you could potentially beat the throw."
It was a sublime bit of baserunning, the kind that takes years of purposeful, monotonous practice to get good at. There's also an element of internal pre-pitch preparation: "If X happens, I do Y." Yelich executed that process perfectly. Caminero, who had ample time to get the slow-footed Contreras at first, did not.
"The beauty of it is that you have guys like Yeli that demand it from the group," first-base coach Spencer Allen told Yahoo Sports about the team's attention to detail.
Jason Lane, Milwaukee's offense and strategy coordinator, explained to Yahoo Sports that he tells players to approach a secondary lead at first base and two outs with the same intent and intensity they would bring to a "contact play." That's the inside-baseball term for when a runner at third, with the infield drawn in, plans to race home on contact — no matter where the ball's hit.
"When you remind guys of that and explain it to them like that — and these guys are hunting all those little things that we preach about right turns — it can become something that happens in a playoff game," he explained.
On a team that cares deeply about the little things, Yelich, the group's most accomplished character, might care most of all. That establishes a standard, one that has helped push the Brewers to an amazing 10-1 record this postseason. But that crucial play, and its outcome, was about more than Yelich's impressive read and instincts. His footspeed from first to second clocked in at 28.5 mph, a full tick faster than his season average. That's an 81st-percentile result from a 34-year-old DH with a history of back problems.
Yelich was once a speedster before age and injuries did their thing. There exists a timeline in which the 2018 MVP evolved into a bat-first baseclogger, a plodder focused on in-box responsibilities. Instead, Yelich has done everything in his power to remain as athletic, as lithe and as quick as possible. Years of treatment, offseason sprint work, healthy habits, weight room sessions — all of it has allowed Yelich to maintain his speed despite the barrage of injuries and his status as a primary DH.
"I've got some things that have happened to me, but for the most part, I feel pretty good," he said when asked about his speed. "I feel like I can still hang with the boys out there."
The boys agree.
"That baserunning by Yeli there, which allowed us to have that huge inning ..." outfielder Sal Frelick said. "We work on those things in spring. He's the guy that's running the meeting, saying this is important. It's his 14th season. He's been All-Star, Silver Slugger, MVP, and nobody cares about baserunning more than him. Just to see him do that, get a good secondary, run as hard as he could and beat that out — that's what allowed us to have that big inning."
"Little things like that — that's what makes our team great."
Great might be an understatement. If the Brewers finish the deal in Game 4, they would become the first team in the League Championship Series era to sweep both the championship series and World Series rounds. They would finish this month a mind-boggling 11-1, with their only defeat coming by one run in NLDS Game 3 in San Diego. There's a strong argument that we are currently witnessing the most dominant postseason team in MLB history.
The gap between these Brewers and the rest of the league is a massive chasm, yes, but it's one they chiseled one swing and one step at a time.

MILWAUKEE (AP) — Trevor Megill was shouting in celebration and the Milwaukee Brewers were bolting out of the dugout to congratulate one another, believing they had just escaped a ninth-inning jam to win Game 1 of the World Series.
Not quite yet.
What initially was ruled a game-ending double play got overturned after a video review showed Brewers shortstop Cooper Pratt’s right foot was slightly off the bag when he reached to catch a high throw from second baseman Brice Turang.
No problem.
Megill regrouped and struck out Jonny DeLuca with two runners in scoring position as Milwaukee edged the Tampa Bay Rays 3-2 on Friday night.
“It’s good to get the first win out of the way,” Megill said. “That’s where all the nerves are at. First game, a lot of anticipation and build-up to where we are right now.”
The ninth inning was particularly nerve-racking for the Brewers and the sellout crowd attending Milwaukee’s first World Series game since 1982.
“You have a big range of emotions,” said team captain Christian Yelich, whose RBI triple in the first put the Brewers ahead for good. “It’s a big credit to Trev for locking back in right there and making some huge pitches after you have that emotional dump and then have to get back on it.”
Tampa Bay trailed 3-1 and hadn’t put a runner on since the sixth until it mounted its comeback attempt against Megill.
Jonathan Aranda, who went 3 for 3 with a walk, and Chandler Simpson hit consecutive one-out singles. A double steal involving pinch-runner Jorge Mateo and Simpson put runners on second and third before Junior Caminero walked on a 3-2 pitch in the dirt to load the bases.
Liam Hicks hit a grounder to the right side, and Turang ranged well to his left to field the ball before throwing to Pratt to start what initially was called a 4-6-3 double play.
Fireworks went off, players poured onto the field and Milwaukee fans roared. But then the crowd hushed as it watched the play again on the videoboard.
“You’ve got to think worst-case scenario there,” Megill said. “I thought the challenge was at first base, maybe a bobble or something. But it was pretty clear once the replay went up that it was on the play at second base. Zoomed in and it didn’t look good. It’s all right. We picked up Cooper there. He’ll pick us up tomorrow.”
The out call at second was changed to safe by umpire Alfonso Márquez at the MLB Replay Center, which caught Pratt by surprise.
“Obviously, it was close,” the 22-year-old rookie said. “I just didn’t think it was enough to overturn, so I wasn’t thinking anything of it. The video I saw, thought my cleat was dragging. … There must have been some other angles that I haven’t seen. It ultimately didn’t matter because we won.”
The Brewers won because Megill got DeLuca to swing and miss at a 2-2 pitch, capping a night in which Tampa Bay went 0 for 6 with runners in scoring position.
“This is an extremely confident group,” Rays manager Kevin Cash said. “You know that. We know that. They’re going to be fine. I think the frustration comes from we were one swing of the bat away right at the end of potentially taking the lead.”
The Game 1 winner has gone on to win the World Series 62.8% of the time.
This marks the first World Series featuring two teams seeking their first championship since 1980, when the Philadelphia Phillies beat the Kansas City Royals in six games. The only other major league clubs without a World Series title are the Colorado Rockies, San Diego Padres and Seattle Mariners.
Milwaukee took a 2-0 lead in the first inning against Nick Martinez. NL Cy Young Award favorite Jacob Misiorowski allowed one run and four hits over five innings to help the Brewers stay in front before relievers Abner Uribe and Aaron Ashby shut down the Rays through the eighth.
Misiorowski, who had a season-low three strikeouts, opened the game with a 103.5 mph fastball — the fastest pitch ever thrown in a World Series.
“The adrenaline kind of took over, and I tensed up and threw it hard,” said Misiorowski, who earned the win. “Then I settled down, and that was the game plan, to settle in and do me. Don’t try and overdo it.”
Milwaukee’s Jackson Chourio and William Contreras each had two hits, including an RBI single. Contreras also threw out two runners trying to steal.
Tampa Bay managed to hang around thanks in part to Martinez, who gave up those two runs in the first but held Milwaukee scoreless through the rest of his five-inning stint. The Brewers added an insurance run in the seventh when Chourio singled home Pratt.
Then came all the action in the ninth, with the Brewers’ premature celebration followed by a team-wide sigh of relief as Pratt offered some parting words to Megill.
“I just said, ‘Thank you, man. Thanks for picking me up,’” Pratt said. “That’s what this game is. It’s a game of pick-me-up. He picked me up today.”
Up next
Drew Rasmussen (16-5, 2.67 ERA) pitches for Tampa Bay and Logan Henderson (11-3, 2.47) starts for Milwaukee in Game 2 on Saturday night. In this postseason, Rasmussen is 2-0 with a 1.29 ERA and Henderson is 0-0 with a 3.00 ERA.

MILWAUKEE (AP) — The Miz will try to whiz his famous fastball by batters on baseball's biggest stage, opening a new-look World Series between teams guaranteed to produce a first-time champion.
Jacob Misiorowski brings his record-setting heat to the mound for the Milwaukee Brewers on Friday night when he throws the first pitch of the best-of-seven championship against the Tampa Bay Rays, a matchup of modest-money marvels who bumped off glamorous rivals with a throwback base-to-base style.
“Forrest Gump, everyone,” Brewers manager Pat Murphy said Thursday, introducing his ace to the assembled media.
“I'm still fresh to all of this and I have no idea what the hell is going on,” Misiorowski said a few minutes later.
Few predicted this pairing of pennant winners when the season opened March 25. The first World Series with robot umpires is the first since 1980 between teams seeking their first championship and also could be the first with a 104 mph pitch — thanks to Misiorowski — and the first to be played totally indoors.
Milwaukee is in the Series for the second time after a 44-year absence — an appropriate number given that it was the jersey of the Cream City's most famous baseball player, Hank Aaron, who became a star with the Milwaukee Braves in the 1950s and ended his career with the expansion Brewers in the 1970s.
Both teams fell short in previous Series trips, the Brewers losing to St. Louis in 1982 and the Rays to Philadelphia in 2008 and to the Los Angeles Dodgers in 2020. Not since the Phillies beat Kansas City in 1980 have two teams met seeking their first title. The time before that was in 1920.
Rays players are excited to display their brand of baseball.
“We love watching those guys cause chaos,” Tampa Bay pitcher Steven Matz said of his team's bunters and speedsters. “Every time it’s first and third and someone lays down a bunt, we are just dying laughing in the bullpen.”
Misiorowski is likely to set a World Series velocity record
Misiorowski, a 24-year-old right-hander in his first full major league season, is a starting pitcher like no other. He threw 1,115 pitches of 100 mph or higher this year — shattering the old high of 673 since tracking began in 2008, by Jordan Hicks in 2018.
His fastest pitch was 105.5 mph to the Chicago Cubs' Pete Crow-Armstrong on June 27, and he appears likely to break the 101.1 mph record for a Series starter by the New York Mets' Noah Syndergaard in 2015 and possibly the overall Series high of 103.2 mph by Cubs reliever Aroldis Chapman to Cleveland's Coco Crisp in Game 2 of 2016.
Misiorowski didn't finish the fifth inning in either of his first two postseason starts this year. Batters have swung at 94 of his 182 postseason pitches and fouled off 51 — 28% of pitches and 54% of swings.
“He hasn’t been as crisp,” Murphy said. “They’re obviously looking at an area. They’re trying to exploit everything. He’s exposed, like all these guys get at some point.”
Martinez a surprise starter for Rays
Nick Martinez will start for Tampa Bay, which gives extra rest to Drew Rasmussen ahead of Game 2 and Freddy Peralta before Game 3.
A 36-year-old right-hander with his fourth major league team, Martinez took the Rays to dinner Wednesday at Carnevor, a top Milwaukee steakhouse. He invites teammates, who have nicknamed him “El Presidente,” to a restaurant in every road city.
“To when I first got to the league, I’ve been around guys that knew how to control a clubhouse and for lack of a better term, knew how to throw a party,” Martinez said. “Getting the guys together is important. Creating that off-the-field chemistry translates to on the field.”
Brewers and Rays have throwback offenses
In an age where power bats usually rule, Milwaukee scored a major league-low 32.1% of its runs on homers and Tampa Bay was second-lowest at 34.4%, according to the Elias Sports Bureau.
Brewers captain Christian Yelich says “we’ve done a good job of being kind of chameleons.”
“It's cool that you don't have to be the team to hit 170 home runs a game or whatever,” Misiorowski said. “You can win a baseball game so many different ways.”
Rays batters had the fewest strikeouts among the 30 teams and Tampa Bay’s 45 sacrifice bunts were the most among American League teams since 2015.
“If we had a club that was built with a bunch of boppers, we probably wouldn’t be bunting and stealing bases,” Rays manager Kevin Cash said. “I think we already have made bunting cool.”
After back-to-back Dodgers titles, MLB will have a small-payroll champion
This marks the first time since 1991 that both Series teams are in the bottom half of payrolls: the Brewers were 19th as of Aug. 31 and the Rays 25th. Milwaukee, MLB's smallest market, could become the first small-market champion since Kansas City in 2015. The Rays rank 15th in market size.
To reach the Series, the Brewers swept the deep-pocketed, two-time champion Dodgers in the NL Championship Series and the Rays swept the New York Yankees in an AL Division Series.
Yelich, the highest-paid player in the Series, was 44th overall in the majors on opening day. Yandy Díaz, who earns most among the Rays, ranked 154th.
Robot umps are changing games
Batters have succeeded on 63% of challenges during the postseason in the first year of the Automated Ball-Strike System, winning 40 of 63 appeals to the robot umps. That is up from 49% during the regular season.
Catchers' 58% success rate in the playoffs (58 of 99) is down a tick from 59% during the regular season and pitchers are 1 for 1 — Tampa Bay’s Griffin Jax made the only challenge. The 60% overall rate is up from 54% in the regular season.
Tampa Bay's batters have yet to make a postseason challenge. Milwaukee's have won 4 of 7, including a perfect 2 for 2 by Jake Bauers.
Brewers catcher William Contreras has won 60% (12 of 20) and Rays catcher Liam Hicks 67% (8 of 12).
Rest vs. rust: Extra time off hasn't been helpful in recent years
Milwaukee will have had seven days off going into the opener.
While teams with less rest are 15-15 in the Series since Wild Card Era started in 1995, they are 12-4 since 2009.
___
Ronald Blum, The Associated Press

The 2026 World Series is going to make history. Either the Tampa Bay Rays or Milwaukee Brewers are about to claim their first championship.
So, that's what's at stake. But what should everyone expect?
According to FanDuel, the Brewers are the favorite (-172) and the Rays are the underdog (+148). Yet this is ultimately a 103-win team against a 98-win team, and both clubs play a very similar style of baseball.
It's therefore worth getting in depth with the specifics of this matchup before making any predictions. Who are the key players? What are the key matchups? What are the X-factors that will determine the series?
Let's see what we can see, and then we'll present picks for the winner of the World Series and for the World Series MVP.
World Series Schedule
1 of 6
All Games on Fox
Game 1 (Friday, October 23): Tampa Bay at Milwaukee, 8:00 p.m. ET
Game 2 (Saturday, October 24): Tampa Bay at Milwaukee, 8:00 p.m. ET
Game 3 (Monday, October 26): Milwaukee at Tampa Bay, 8:00 p.m. ET
Game 4 (Tuesday, October 27): Milwaukee at Tampa Bay, 8:00 p.m. ET
Game 5 (Wednesday, October 28)*: Milwaukee at Tampa Bay, 8:00 p.m. ET
Game 6 (Friday, October 30)*: Tampa Bay at Milwaukee, 8:00 p.m. ET
Game 7 (Saturday, October 31)*: Tampa Bay at Milwaukee, 8:00 p.m. ET
*If necessary
Key Players for the Rays
2 of 6
3B Junior Caminero
Caminero has been the driving force in the Rays' lineup over the last two seasons, slamming over 40 home runs and racking up over 100 RBI in each. Yet he went cool with a season-low .772 OPS in September, and he initially struggled to snap out of it once the postseason began.
That changed in the last three games of the ALCS. The 23-year-old had hits in all three, including a home run in the clincher that he soaked in as much as possible (and then some). Is he back? It sure seems like he's back.
DH Yandy Díaz
Even if he's not as big of a power threat as Caminero, Díaz rarely fails to have a good at-bat or to hit the ball on a line. He's hit an even .300 across the last four seasons, and he led the AL in hits this year.
The 35-year-old was not the MVP of the ALCS, but he could have been. He torched the Cleveland Guardians for a 1.061 OPS and six extra-base hits, culminating in the two-run homer that iced Game 6.
RHP Drew Rasmussen
Even if he didn't get a ton of hype, Rasmussen was a ball-knower's ace in the regular season between 2022 and 2026. He posted a sub-3.00 ERA annually, and he even led the AL in WHIP this season.
Now the secret is out. The 31-year-old's three starts in the playoffs have yielded just three earned runs in 21.0 innings, with 23 strikeouts and only three walks. His changeup has been especially lethal, holding hitters to three hits in 24 at-bats.
RHP Freddy Peralta
Peralta was with the Brewers this time last year, and his journey since then has taken him to lows with the New York Mets and now highs again with the Rays. He's coming into the World Series hot off being named the ALCS MVP.
The 30-year-old doesn't offer a complicated scouting report. He's throwing his fastball about 70 percent of the time in October, daring hitters to beat him on his best pitch. They haven't, going just 8-for-39 against it so far.
RHP Bryan Baker
Baker blew his third save of the year back on May 13. He hasn't blown one since in 53 turns on the mound, along the way allowing just five earned runs in 52.0 innings.
The 31-year-old's velocity has declined throughout the year, but that has yet to translate into any kind of advantage for hitters. It could be because he uses his fastball and changeup in roughly equal tandem, using both to hold hitters to one hit in 21 at-bats thus far in October.
Key Players for the Brewers
3 of 6
LF Jackson Chourio
The Brewers signed Chourio to an $84 million contract before he had played even one game in the majors. It has paid off in the form of three straight 20-20 seasons, and all before he's turned even 23 years old.
On paper, his .171 batting average and .553 OPS say he's not having a good postseason. Yet even if the Brewers would like more consistency, they'll take the clutch gene that has delivered seven RBI, including two that snatched victory from the jaws of defeat.
1B Jake Bauers
There were 137 players who took at least 500 plate appearances this season, and only 12 of them had a better OPS+ than Bauers. Not bad for a 31-year-old who had an 84 OPS+ for his career coming into the season.
Bauers has become a menace of another sort in the playoffs. Even if he only has one multi-hit game, he's shown tremendous patience in racking up a .441 OBP and driving in six runs. He had multiple at-bats that dug the Los Angeles Dodgers' grave as he was winning MVP honors for the NLCS.
C William Contreras
Contreras has regressed a little as a regular-season performer, but you'd never know from how he's hit this postseason. He's hit safely in six of eight games, with three home runs and five RBI.
Also, don't overlook his mastery of the ABS. He challenged a league-high 185 calls from behind the plate this season, and he won 80 of them. He's kept it up in the playoffs, going 8-for-12 and winning some truly game-changing challenges.
RHP Jacob Misiorowski
After making 30 starts and pitching to a 1.80 ERA and a 5.7 K/BB ratio, Misiorowski is going to win the NL Cy Young Award. As soon as he hit 104.8 mph on his first pitch of the playoffs, he seemed ready to tap into still another gear for October.
Except, he hasn't made it past the fifth inning in either of his two assignments, consisting of nine hits and four walks in 8.1 total innings. He clearly isn't gassed, but he'll need to be better to maximize Milwaukee's chances in the World Series.
LHP Aaron Ashby
Milwaukee's entire bullpen has been incredible in the playoffs, handling 40.2 innings and allowing just six earned runs. Trevor Megill and Abner Uribe deserve their flowers, too.
Yet Ashby has simply been on another level, thus far posting 12.1 shutout innings and allowing just four hits and three walks. The next hitter who gets a knock off his curveball, changeup or slider will be the first.
Matchups That Will Define the World Series
4 of 6
Junior Caminero's Bat Speed vs. the Brewers' Velocity
What makes Caminero so dangerous? For one thing, nobody whips the bat through the zone like he does. His average swing this season was 79.5 mph, the highest of any qualified hitter.
In the World Series, though, he'll be up against a Brewers pitching staff that is averaging 98.3 mph on the fastball. That's almost a full mile per hour faster than the hardest-throwing staff of the 2025 playoffs.
Chandler Simpson's Speed vs. the Brewers' Defenders
Simpson is basically a free 90 feet in human form. He had 11 more infield hits than anyone else this season. He also stole 46 bases, and took 21 more bases on wild pitches, passed balls and the like. It all makes him a rare weapon.
The Brewers, though, could be up to stopping him. Their infield was among the very best this season with a total output of +7 Outs Above Average. More to the point, William Contreras was second in the league in caught-stealings.
Jacob Misiorowski vs. the Rays' High-Contact Offense
Misiorowski's contact rate during the regular season was a mere 65.5 percent, easily the best in baseball. Yet he hasn't been nearly as successful at avoiding contact in the postseason, where his rate has jumped to 77.4 percent.
If the San Diego Padres and Los Angeles Dodgers could do that, the Rays should be able to as well. They led MLB with an 81.8 contact percentage during the regular season, and it has only gone down to 77.2 in the postseason.
The Brewers' Lefty Bats vs. the Rays' Righty-Heavy Pitching
It isn't just Jake Bauers. Milwaukee's left-handed hitters as a collective have a 122 wRC+ in the playoffs, and that's despite facing some darn good left-handed pitching. In the NLCS alone, they faced a pair of two-time Cy Young Award winners in Tarik Skubal and Blake Snell.
The Rays aren't nearly as synonymous with left-handed pitching, indeed carrying only three for the ALCS against Cleveland. And one of them (Ian Seymour) isn't looking so hot after carrying a heavy workload in the regular season.
X-Factors That Will Define the World Series
5 of 6
Home Cooking
The best home record in MLB during the regular season? Well, it was a tie at 55-26… between the Rays and Brewers, naturally.
Neither club has fumbled its home-field advantage in the postseason. The Brewers are 4-0 at American Family Field. The Rays are 4-1 at Tropicana Field. So on paper, both teams can claim to have an advantage on their home turf.
That said, it's the Brewers who truly stand to find out. If this series goes the distance, they'll have the honor of hosting the finale in Milwaukee on October 31.
The Three True Outcomes
For the uninitiated, the three true outcomes are strikeouts, walks and home runs. Neither the Rays nor the Brewers was necessarily synonymous with the concept during the regular season, specifically in the sense that they both ranked in the bottom 10 of the league in home runs.
They have since gone on wildly different paths in October. The Brewers' percentage of three true outcomes when on offense is at 47 percent. For the Rays, it's only 31 percent.
Both paths have ultimately arrived in the same spot, but this may be where we find out which one wins the day. Can the Brewers keep winning by racking up walks and homers? Or, will the Rays avoid enough strikeouts to gain the inside track?
Speed and Defense
Regardless of what happens in the TTO department, neither of these teams should be expected to give much away, while both should be expected to take as much as they can get.
In other words, they're both good at fielding the ball and running the bases. The Rays and Brewers each ranked in the top six for defensive efficiency this season. They were both top-five in stolen bases, and separated by just two steals in the end.
In these respects, the World Series should reward baseball purists for their attention. The result could come down to fine margins—a ball just out of reach or a tag applied just in time.
Predicting the Outcome and World Series MVP
6 of 6
For the World Series: Brewers in 6
Regarding my credentials, I had the Brewers sweeping the Dodgers in the NLCS before it happened. So, I've been right at least once in my life.
Yet whereas the Dodgers looked old, slow and generally out of sorts while trying to keep pace with Milwaukee, the Rays are cut from the same cloth as a ballclub. They're younger and more athletic, and committed to playing smart, clean baseball that emphasizes the little things to add up to one big haymaker.
One area where Milwaukee should have an edge is on offense. The Brewers have as many as five hitters you really have to worry about. The Rays really only have three, in Junior Caminero, Yandy Díaz and Jonathan Aranda.
The Brewers' bullpen stands out as another advantage, even if they'll need more from their starters to avoid their relievers getting overexposed in a longer series. It, too, is deeper than what the Rays have to offer. And let's be real that Milwaukee relievers are simply on a heater right now.
So, congratulations in advance to the Brewers. If anything is worth a 57-year wait, it's a World Series championship.
For World Series MVP: William Contreras
This pick is partially about deferring to a hot hand. The Brewers have gotten contributions from all their hitters in the postseason, but Contreras has been a constant the whole way through. You just can't fake a 1.157 OPS.
Between his ABS challenges and his ability to control the running game, Contreras' defense also stands to be a huge factor in the World Series. He could also be a not-so-secret weapon when Freddy Peralta pitches for the Rays. If anyone knows him, it's the guy who caught him 81 times between 2023 and 2025.

Juan Soto
had a short message for Freddy Peralta after the Tampa Bay Rays star won the 2026 American League Championship Series (ALCS) MVP award on Monday. The New York Mets outfielder shared two comments on his Instagram story as the Rays beat the Cleveland Guardians 7-3 in Game 6 to reach the World Series. Soto’s words came after Peralta turned his season around following a trade from New York to Tampa Bay in August. The pitcher’s strong playoff run has now earned him one of baseball’s biggest postseason awards.
Juan Soto’s Instagram Messages Follow Freddy Peralta’s ALCS MVP Award
Soto shared two messages in Spanish on his Instagram story on Monday. One read, “Did I tell you so or what?” The second said, “the best in the classroom 🔥,” according to the English translations provided.
The comments came on the same day Peralta received the ALCS MVP award after helping Tampa Bay win the series against Cleveland. The Rays took the series 4-2 and claimed their third American League pennant. They last reached the World Series in 2020.
Peralta was once Soto’s teammate with the Mets. However, New York traded the right-handed pitcher to Tampa Bay on August 2 after a difficult first part of the season.
Soto had his own challenges in 2026. The five-time All-Star hit .275 with 27 home runs but missed several games because of a calf strain.
His brief messages put the focus on Peralta’s big achievement, which came after a major change in teams and a much stronger finish to the season.
How Freddy Peralta Turned His Season Around With the Tampa Bay Rays
Peralta struggled during his time with the Mets. He went 5-9 with a 4.99 ERA across 22 starts in New York. After joining Tampa Bay, he recorded a 3.25 ERA over his final 10 regular-season starts, giving the Rays a much stronger option on the mound.
His work against Cleveland in the ALCS was even better. Peralta finished with a 0.75 ERA, nine strikeouts and just one run allowed over 12 innings. He won twice and also made a short relief appearance during the series.
In Game 6 on Monday, Peralta allowed one run over 5 1/3 innings as Tampa Bay secured a 7-3 victory at Tropicana Field. His performance helped the Rays finish off the Guardians and book their place in the World Series.
After receiving the award, Peralta summed up his feelings in a few words.
“This is crazy,” he said, before thanking the people around him.
“I’m very happy to be here, to be part of this great group and this organization. Milwaukee is always going to be in my heart, but it’s time to compete.”
The Associated Press and MLB.com reported on Peralta’s reaction after the game. CBS Sports also reported his ALCS MVP win and his strong postseason performance.
Peralta spent his first eight seasons with the Milwaukee Brewers before moving to the Mets in January. New York then traded him to Tampa Bay in August. Now, he will face his former Milwaukee team in the World Series.
The matchup gives Peralta a chance to compete for a championship against the club where he began his major league career. For the Rays, his late-season improvement has helped carry them to baseball’s biggest stage.

item.content:encoded:
Just days ago, the Tampa Bay Rays were trailing the Cleveland Guardians in the ALCS two games to one. Three straight wins later, they're back in the World Series for the second time in seven years and the third time in franchise history.
Which means that now, our 2026 Fall Classic is officially set. And while it might not be the big-market showdown of Rob Manfred's dreams, it should be absolutely box-office baseball, as the two best teams of this season square off to try and make franchise history. Let's dive in.
Updated MLB playoff bracket after Rays advance to the World Series
And then there were two. The Milwaukee Brewers punched their ticket to the World Series seemingly eons ago, dispatching of the Los Angeles Dodgers in a shocking sweep. Now that the Rays have knocked off the Guardians in the ALCS, our World Series matchup is set.
- World Series: Tampa Bay Rays (AL champs) vs. Milwaukee Brewers (NL champs)
It's not all that often that the top seed in each league meets in the Fall Classic; baseball's postseason is notoriously unpredictable. But these teams won 98 and 103 games in the regular season, respectively, and led the AL and NL more or less wire-to-wire. They were the best in baseball, and they proved as much in October. Now it's time to see which will make history and capture their franchise's first-ever World Series title.
Full World Series schedule: Milwaukee will be rocking for Game 1
We'll have a few days of waiting: Game 1 is set for Friday, Oct. 23, with first pitch from American Family Field in Milwaukee at 8 p.m. ET. The series will follow the traditional 2-3-2 format, with days off for travel after Games 2 and 5. Games 1, 2, 6 and 7 will be in Milwaukee, with Games 3-5 in Tampa.
| Game | Location | Date | Time |
|---|---|---|---|
| Game 1 | American Family Field | Friday, Oct. 23 | 8 p.m. ET |
| Game 2 | American Family Field | Saturday, Oct. 24 | 8 p.m. ET |
| Game 3 | Tropicana Field | Monday, Oct. 26 | 8 p.m. ET |
| Game 4 | Tropicana Field | Tuesday, Oct. 27 | 8 p.m. ET |
| Game 5 | Tropicana Field | Wednesday, Oct. 28 | 8 p.m. ET |
| Game 6 | American Family Field | Friday, Oct. 30 | 8 p.m. ET |
| Game 7 | American Family Field | Saturday, Oct. 31 | 8 p.m. ET |
The Rays are grateful for the break, as it will allow them to reset their pitching staff and line ace Drew Rasmussen up to face off against Jacob Misiorowski in Game 1. Clinching on Monday also allows Freddy Peralta to potentially get the ball in Game 2 on Saturday on full rest, with Nick Martinez likely behind him in Game 3.
Of course, the last thing the Brewers need is more rest. They clinched the NLCS in Game 4 last Thursday, Oct. 15, meaning they've already been at home for four days. By the time Game 1 of the World Series rolls around, it'll have been over a week since they last played a competitive game. Rust is overblown this time of year, but it's still something to monitor.
How to watch the 2026 World Series
This year's World Series will be broadcast exclusively on FOX.
- Dates: Oct. 23-Oct. 31
- TV channel: FOX
- Streaming: FOX One, YouTube TV, Hulu + Live Sports
You can also stream all the action on FOX One, provided you have a Fox One subscription ($19.99/month) or a valid cable login. You can also stream FOX through a variety of platforms, from YouTube TV to Hulu to Sling TV — all of which have free trials for new customers.
Pitching and power will define Brewers-Rays matchup
Suffice to say that runs are going to be at a premium in this series. Milwaukee ranked second in baseball in team ERA during the regular season, while the Rays were seventh. With Misiorowski, Logan Henderson and the best bullpen in baseball on one side and Rasmussen, Peralta, Martinez and All-Star closer Bryan Baker on the other, these teams have arms for days.
As such, it's going to be awfully hard to string together rallies — which means the team that finds a way to access some power will be at a distinct advantage. Neither team played much long ball during the regular season; both ranked in the bottom third of the league in homers, and neither ranked in the top 10 in slugging percentage. But the Brewers actually outslugged the big, bad Dodgers in the NLCS, and the Rays pulled away from Cleveland when their big bats (Junior Caminero, Yandy Diaz and Jonathan Aranda) finally found the power stroke.
There won't be a ton of homers in this series. But whichever team has the most will almost certainly be hoisting the Commissioner's Trophy when all is said and done. If you're trying to play small ball against Abner Uribe, good luck.

Alejandro Kirk has always been one of the most likeable players in the Toronto Blue Jays clubhouse. His steady presence, team-first approach and easygoing personality have made him a trusted teammate. But Kirk’s “Mr. Nice Guy” influence isn't limited to the guys who wear the same uniform as him.
It has extended across the American League East, where Kirk’s longtime friend Jonathan Aranda is trying to help the Tampa Bay Rays capture their first World Series title.
With the pressure of the postseason mounting, Aranda turned to his childhood friend who had just lived through the grind of a pressure packed postseason. During the Blue Jays’ run to the 2025 World Series Kirk played in all 18 games and slashed .254/.349/.493 with a 132 wRC+ and five home runs.
“I was like, ‘Hey, do you have any tips for me moving forward here in October?’ And his main suggestion was, just have fun, just have fun and be yourself,” Aranda told Sportsnet’s Shi Davidi through interpreter Kevin Vera ahead of Game 5 of the ALCS. “That's honestly helped me a lot to kind of slow the game down and enjoy the moment and embrace this challenge of what is October baseball.”
That advice could not have come at a better time for the Rays' Aranda who went 0-for-10 through the first three games of the best-of-seven series against the Cleveland Guardians. Then in Game 4 he broke out with three hits, a walk, two RBI and two runs scored in the Rays’ 7-3 win.
Kirk’s advice allowed Arenda some time to reflect on the process how to revive himself and be the player everyone expected him to be. He encouraged Aranda to trust himself and remember why he was there. The 28-year-old first baseman hit 22 home runs during the regular season while slashing .274/.358/.434 with a 123 wRC+ and a13.8 offensive fWAR.
Longtime friends Alejandro Kirk and Jonathan Aranda have always supported each other
For Kirk, helping a player on a division rival didn't seem like a conflict considering the Blue Jays bowed out of the postseason before it even began. Aranda said the two “talk every day, we're best friends, we're brothers,” adding that Kirk is “someone that I have by my side.”
The support has always worked both ways. When the Blue Jays advanced to the World Series last year, Aranda flew in to support Kirk, saying “it was a big thing for me to go see him, for us, to see each other in the World Series.”
Watching Kirk make history on baseball’s biggest stage gave Aranda a chance to picture himself playing October baseball. He said, “In that moment last year, I kind of visualized myself in the same scenario. So now, fast-forward a year later, I use it as motivation right now. Hopefully I can make those dreams that I had last year a reality and help this team to a World Series berth.”
The Blue Jays would rather see their own players carrying Kirk’s lessons deep into October. Still, his role in Aranda’s run says something meaningful about Kirk’s off-field qualities that don't show up in the scorebox every day.

item.content:encoded:
Tarik Skubal and the Los Angeles Dodgers were swept out of the NLCS by the 103-win Milwaukee Brewers, a refreshing change of pace after two years of Dodgers dominance — and a helpful reminder to the MLB owners that payroll alone does not determine winning. It also leaves Skubal with a more difficult decision in free agency than many expected.
The Dodgers will not re-sign Skubal before the lockout in December, as there's simply too much risk without knowing how the salary cap will function come 2027. Really regardless of how MLB's labor dispute plays out, however, Los Angeles will hope to retain Skubal, who is still rightly regarded as the most bankable ace in baseball. The question is: Are the Dodgers the favorites for his services? Let's rank all realistic suitors, from least to most realistic.
8. Philadelphia Phillies
The Phillies are desperate and the Phillies typically spend money. Not necessarily as liberally as fans would like, but it's not impossible to imagine Dave Dombrowski — with the World Series window closing rapidly on this aging core — deciding that Skubal is worth an all-in push.
It would give Philadelphia the most talented rotation in MLB between Skubal, Zack Wheeler, Cristopher Sánchez, Jesús Luzardo and Aaron Nola, four of whom could compete for NL Cy Young next season. There's also Andrew Painter, a former top prospect who came into his own down the stretch and delivered big outs in the postseason, to provide depth.
The Phillies probably have enough money wrapped up in that rotation (and in Bryce Harper, Kyle Schwarber and Trea Turner) to be turned off of paying Skubal top dollar, but it's a fun thought for a team hoping to lean even more on run prevention moving forward.
7. Boston Red Sox
The Red Sox wielded one of the deepest and most reliable rotations in MLB last season; that was with top ace Garrett Crochet on the IL. Upon Crochet's return, Boston will have a compelling blend of experience (Crochet, Ranger Suárez) and emerging youth (Payton Tolle, Jake Bennett) to throw at their opponents.
Then again, they know the toll injuries can take, and Sonny Gray — probably their best regular season starter this past season — is now a free agent. The Red Sox could simply line up a new contract for Gray and be content, but why not aim higher? Skubal has proven remarkably durable over the years and he offers Boston a much longer window as Crochet's partner in crime. Suddenly, the Red Sox have the best one-two punch in baseball and it wouldn't be especially close.
After the Yankees lit them up in the Wild Card round (and after Boston's top arms couldn't pitch deep into either postseason game), there's pressure for a big swing.
6. Chicago Cubs
There's no doubting the Cubs' ability to generate offense, but the rotation has been a sore spot for years now. Jed Hoyer has shown a great appetite for spending in free agency of late; the Alex Bregman signing was a real flex. That said, Chicago needs to allocate more resources toward pitching. The Edward Cabrera trade went belly up. Shōta Imanaga is a free agent now, as are trade deadline pickups Kevin Gausman and Clay Holmes.
Chicago will get help internally with both Cade Horton and Justin Steele returning from season-long elbow injuries; Ben Brown, who finally broke out in 2026, should also be back in the mix. Beyond them, however, it's pretty grim. Matthew Boyd and Javier Assad can eat innings in the regular season, but neither has proven able to pitch deep in October — at least not consistently.
Skubal would deliver Chicago the frontline ace it has long lacked, with a solid scaffolding of talent behind him. The Cubs would be much better positioned to challenge Milwaukee in the division and potentially emerge from a crowded National League field.
5. Detroit Tigers
Skubal has made it clear he would've spent his entire career in Detroit if it was up to him. All the Tigers need to do is come through with a competitive offer. While last year's surprise Framber Valdez signing was a positive indication of the front office's competitive intent, there's a reason no Skubal extension ever came to fruition — or even remotely close.
A client of Scott Boras, Skubal was never inclined to sign an extension. But the Tigers' offers weren't even in the parking lot, much less the ballpark. Detroit will need to scale up its ambition significantly if it wants to lure Skubal back to the midwest.
All that said, Skubal has an affection for Detroit that's worth mentioning. The Tigers also desperately need a frontline ace in Skubal's mold. Young bucks like Troy Melton, Keider Montero, Jackson Jobe and River Ryan are very talented, but the Tigers don't really have an established vet besides Valdez, who was a mess last season.
4. New York Yankees
The Yankees tend to flex their muscles in free agency, although with diminishing returns in recent years. New York is no longer the most lucrative destination for a lot of A-tier stars. Juan Soto a couple years ago, Kyle Tucker last winter; the Yankees are getting outbid pretty consistently these days. That has not stopped New York from stockpiling stars, though, especially in the rotation.
It would require Hal Steinbrenner and the front office to basically sign off on a blank check, but the Yankees' ALDS loss to the Rays was a sobering defeat. There are cracks in the foundation. Many of those cracks are injury-related and concentrated in the lineup; Cam Schlittler, Max Fried, Gerrit Cole and Carlos Rodón is as strong a four-man gauntlet as any rotation in MLB. The Yankees also have Ryan Weathers, Will Warren and top prospects like Elmer Rodríguez and Carlos Lagrange for depth.
Still, the Yankees know the importance of depth, especially as their non-Schlittler core ages and becomes more injury-prone. Skubal provides stability and instantly lends credibility to any postseason aspirations. Schlittler-Skubal becomes the most fearsome pitching duo in baseball. Never say never.
3. Toronto Blue Jays
The Blue Jays have steadily become the most aggressive front office in the American League. After finishing runner-up in the Juan Soto and Shohei Ohtani sweepstakes, Toronto extended Vladimir Guerrero Jr. at a $500 million price point and signed Dylan Cease in the early days of free agency last winter. A disappointing season should not preclude Toronto from maintaining its all-in approach; if anything, it's more motivation for the Blue Jays to stack talent. This team was in the World Series a year ago.
Toronto is a great market, with a vibrant local culture and an entire country behind the Blue Jays. That ought to appeal to the vanity of a star like Skubal, who would team up with the projected AL Cy Young runner-up in Cease. The Jays also made a savvy trade for José Soriano at the deadline, adding another premium arm in his prime. Trey Yesavage, once healthy, could resume his ascent to stardom. The talent is there.
Skubal solidifies Toronto as a legitimate World Series contender coming into 2027. Moreover, the Jays have a lot of money coming off the books, which should free up the front office to spend recklessly where it counts. Toronto is always the "dark horse" in these top-dollar bidding wars, but ruling out the Blue Jays would be foolish.
2. Los Angeles Dodgers
It's impossible to rule out the incumbents. Los Angeles made the Skubal trade in part because of their deep farm system — and in part because it set the stage for a potential long-term partnership. There's a reason small-market front offices were unwilling to match L.A.'s outgoing package (see: Brewers). The Dodgers could afford to trade two of the 50ish best prospects in baseball because the team can feel reasonably good about both competing for a World Series this season (oh well) and re-signing Skubal when he hits the open market.
An NLCS loss does complicate the situation somewhat, not to mention the unknowability of upcoming labor disputes. The Dodgers' loss was a direct result of investing hundreds of millions of dollars in stars who are beginning to decline. Mookie Betts, Freddie Freeman, Shohei Ohtani, Will Smith, Tyler Glasnow and Blake Snell are all on the wrong side of 30; Tucker will join that list next season. Los Angeles will endure more and more diminishing returns.
That said, nothing (besides a strict salary cap) can really stop the Dodgers from compensating for declining stars by signing more expensive stars, even if it leaves the cap sheet in utter chaos five years from now. That has been L.A.'s strategy to date; it was part of the logic behind the Skubal trade. The Dodgers still arguably represent Skubal's best chance to win a World Series, which will no doubt be part of the calculus if another team can't dramatically outspend them.
1. New York Mets
If any team can blow L.A.'s offer out of the water, it's the Mets. Steve Cohen is baseball's richest owner and New York has consistently tossed its hat in the ring for MLB's premium free agents. Juan Soto's $765 million contract set a new record; Skubal very well could set a record for pitchers.
The Mets are coming off of a last-place season, too, which only fuels anxiety in the fan base. It should also fuel aggression in the front office. David Stearns is under pressure to prove that he has what it takes to win in New York. Skubal would join an emerging ace in Nolan McLean, plus other whippersnappers like Zac Thornton and Jonah Tong. The Mets need depth besides, as Kodai Senga and Sean Manaea look more like bullpen arms these days. New York, however, is the one non-Dodgers team with enough money to sign Skubal and pursue other targets.
If the Dodgers get spooked by the shadow of their own payroll, which is more likely than ever, the Mets are the logical team we can expect to swoop in and win the Skubal bidding war outright.

item.content:encoded:
When the Brewers finished off the Dodgers on Thursday night, their World Series opponent was the last thing on anyone’s mind. An MLB official closed the postgame press conference by telling manager Pat Murphy and NLCS MVP Jake Bauers, “We’ll see you in Milwaukee at the World Series.”
Murphy’s reply said everything: “When’s that start?”
Next Friday, Oct. 23, at American Family Field, where Milwaukee holds home-field advantage thanks to its franchise-record 103 wins. The Guardians took a 2-1 ALCS lead over the Rays into Friday night's scheduled Game 4 at Progressive Field. Milwaukee, meanwhile, will have a full week to rest, which leaves plenty of time to watch and wonder.
Here’s a guide to each potential matchup. You decide which one you’d rather see.
If the regular season is a guide ...
It doesn’t tell us much. The Brewers went 2-1 against both teams.
Milwaukee won the first two games against Cleveland on June 16-17 before rookie left-hander Parker Messick struck out nine over six innings in the finale. Cleveland was without José Ramírez, Angel Martínez and Chase DeLauter. All three are back.
When the Brewers hit
Milwaukee’s lineup is built on pressure. The Brewers ranked in the top five in doubles, runs, hits, walks, batting average and on-base percentage.
That approach might get more of a test against Tampa Bay. The Rays issued the fewest walks in the Majors (409) and ranked second in defensive runs saved (87). Drawing walks and finding holes gets tougher against that combination. And their top starters have carried it into October: Drew Rasmussen has a 1.29 ERA through two postseason starts, while Peralta has allowed one earned run in 10 2/3 innings, including six shutout innings in Game 2 of the ALCS.
Cleveland offers a different challenge. Gavin Williams has been a monster, striking out 33 over 16 2/3 innings this postseason. The Guardians have a 2.54 ERA this October, slightly better than Tampa Bay’s 2.72. But Cleveland issued 530 regular-season walks to the Rays’ 409, giving Milwaukee more reason to believe its patient approach can create traffic.
When the other side hits
The regular-season numbers favor facing Cleveland. The Guardians had the lowest OPS (.696) and fewest runs (678) of any postseason team. Tampa Bay offered a more complete attack, with Junior Caminero’s 42 homers anchoring a lineup that tied for fifth in on-base percentage (.326).
October has told a different story. Through Thursday, Cleveland was averaging 4.25 runs per game with a .685 OPS, compared with Tampa Bay’s 3.00 runs and .563 OPS. The Guardians haven’t suddenly become an offensive powerhouse, but they’ve been more productive than the Rays, whose lineup managed just three hits in Game 3 of the ALCS.
The larger sample still points toward Cleveland as the preferable opponent. The way these teams are hitting right now makes that a tougher call.
The bullpens
Neither ninth inning looks inviting. Tampa Bay’s Bryan Baker has saved all four Rays wins this postseason without allowing a hit in four innings. Ian Seymour has been a strong bridge, allowing one earned run in 6 1/3 innings.
Cleveland counters with Cade Smith, who has allowed two hits and one run while striking out 13 in nine innings this October. Hunter Gaddis has added six scoreless innings across seven appearances. Both teams have arms capable of shortening games.
The Brewers have made a habit of coming back this postseason, and their bats have shown they can pick at a bullpen late. Against either opponent, getting a lead before the closer enters would make life easier.
What about the intangibles?
The Guardians’ championship drought dates to 1948. The Rays, like the Brewers, have never won a World Series.
The Rays mirror Milwaukee in many ways. Brewers president of baseball operations Matt Arnold worked in Tampa Bay’s front office alongside current Rays GM Erik Neander. Add Peralta facing his former team, and the storyline writes itself.
Cleveland manager Stephen Vogt played for Milwaukee and interviewed for the job that went to Murphy three years ago. And a Cleveland-Milwaukee World Series comes with a built-in movie reference: Major League, filmed in Milwaukee with Bob Uecker’s Harry Doyle calling Cleveland's improbable run.
The verdict
Give the Guardians a slight edge as Milwaukee’s preferred opponent, though their October bats have made that a tougher sell. The Rays were the more complete team over six months. Cleveland has spent the past two weeks making those six months feel a little less relevant.
The Brewers? They just sent the back-to-back champs home. They’ll let the AL sort this out. Somebody remind Murph what time Friday’s game starts.

Dodgers make Tarik Skubal decision that should worry Brewers before NLCS showdown originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The Los Angeles Dodgers are four victories away from returning to the World Series, and manager Dave Roberts has revealed how his team plans to attack the Milwaukee Brewers in the National League Championship Series.
Roberts announced Friday that Tarik Skubal will start Game 1 on Sunday, with Yoshinobu Yamamoto scheduled to pitch Game 2 on Monday. The decision gives Los Angeles two of baseball's most accomplished pitchers to begin a series that features the National League's top two regular-season teams.
The announcement also provides another reminder of the extraordinary pitching depth the Dodgers have assembled. Los Angeles is attempting to win its third consecutive World Series championship, and its starting rotation could become the biggest obstacle standing between Milwaukee and its own championship ambitions.
Tarik Skubal gets another opportunity to set the tone
Skubal will take the mound Sunday at American Family Field after delivering an excellent performance against the Atlanta Braves in the Division Series. The two-time Cy Young Award winner allowed one run on two hits over six innings in Game 1, striking out seven batters while issuing two walks.
Tarik Skubal will start Game 1 with Yoshinobu Yamamoto starting Game 2 for the Dodgers in the NLCS against the Brewers, per @ByJackHarris https://t.co/e8wI91D6uF
— Talkin' Baseball (@TalkinBaseball_) October 9, 2026
Los Angeles acquired Skubal from the Detroit Tigers in a blockbuster August trade, adding another established ace to an already talented pitching staff. His arrival strengthened a rotation that included Yamamoto, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow, giving Roberts multiple options capable of controlling a postseason game.
Starting Skubal in Game 1 is an important decision because Milwaukee owns home-field advantage in the series. The Brewers finished the regular season with 103 victories, while the Dodgers reached the 100-win mark. A strong opening performance would allow Los Angeles to immediately put pressure on a team that has been extremely difficult to beat throughout the year.
Skubal's ability to limit baserunners and generate strikeouts could be particularly valuable against a Milwaukee lineup featuring Christian Yelich, Jackson Chourio and William Contreras.
Yoshinobu Yamamoto gives Dodgers another major advantage
Yamamoto will follow Skubal in Game 2 after producing one of the Dodgers' best pitching performances against Atlanta. The right-hander struck out 10 batters over seven innings, allowing only one run on four hits in a victory that helped Los Angeles regain control of the Division Series.
The performance continued an impressive postseason history for Yamamoto, who earned World Series MVP honors in 2025. His ability to deliver deep, efficient outings gives Roberts another dependable option before the series shifts to Dodger Stadium. Milwaukee is expected to rely heavily on its own talented young pitchers, including Jacob Misiorowski and Logan Henderson. The Brewers have demonstrated throughout the season that they can compete with baseball's most talented rosters, but matching Los Angeles on the mound will be a significant challenge.
The Dodgers also have decisions remaining beyond their first two starters. Roberts indicated Friday that the team was considering adding another pitcher to its NLCS roster, a move that would require removing a position player.
Dodgers still have questions despite pitching advantage
One concern involves veteran utility player Miguel Rojas, who left Game 3 against Atlanta because of lower back discomfort. Rojas participated in baseball activities Friday, but Roberts stopped short of confirming his availability for the championship series.
The Dodgers eliminated Atlanta in four games, while Milwaukee also advanced with a four-game victory over San Diego. The teams now meet in the NLCS for the second consecutive postseason, creating another opportunity for the Brewers to challenge the defending champions. Game 1 is scheduled for Sunday at 8 p.m. ET, with Game 2 following Monday at 5 p.m. ET.
Los Angeles has plenty of offensive talent, including Shohei Ohtani, but its starting pitching could determine how this series unfolds. By sending Skubal and Yamamoto to the mound in Milwaukee, Roberts is giving the Dodgers an opportunity to establish control before returning home.

item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES -- The Dodgers' elite starting pitching was the driving force when they successfully defended their World Series title in 2025. As the back-to-back champions bid for a three-peat, their four-headed monster of a rotation has already been just as impactful four games into their postseason.
Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell, Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Tyler Glasnow recorded a combined 1.69 ERA (four earned runs in 21 1/3 innings) in four games in the NL Division Series against the Braves, the second-lowest mark among this year's postseason rotations. The Rays' starters hold a slight edge with a 1.65 ERA (three earned runs in 16 1/3 innings) in three games.
"To see it play out in the way it did was not surprising," president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman said. "But just the way they went out and competed, the way they challenged each other, we're excited for this next round and for them to get us deep into games and be a huge part of us, hopefully, winning eight more games."
As the second seed in the NL field, the Dodgers had a bye week and were able to reset their rotation to their liking for the postseason. Because they won the NLDS in four games, they'll be able to tweak their starting four again ahead of their NL Championship Series against the Brewers, which begins on Sunday at American Family Field.
With manager Dave Roberts announcing on Friday that Skubal will start Game 1 and Yamamoto Game 2, here's how the Dodgers' rotation could look through the first four games:
Skubal would have started a winner-take-all Game 5 against the Braves on Friday, but the Dodgers took care of business in four. So they'll send their big Trade Deadline reinforcement to the hill for the NLCS opener against the Brewers, who were among the other teams interested in acquiring him this summer.
Milwaukee also has yet to officially announce its rotation order, but Jacob Misiorowski appears lined up to start opposite Skubal, setting up a must-see matchup between the back-to-back AL Cy Young Award winner and this year's presumptive NL Cy Young Award winner.
The Dodgers raised eyebrows by waiting until Game 3 to start Yamamoto in the NLDS. They actually made that decision with the NLCS in mind, as Yamamoto will likely jump ahead of Snell to start Game 2 on his usual five days' rest. Yamamoto would then be available to start a potential Game 6 on his normal rest as well.
Yamamoto has never started on fewer than five days' rest with the Dodgers, but he won last year's World Series MVP honors after closing out Game 7 on zero days' rest. The right-hander said he would be open to pitching on shorter rest and/or in relief again this postseason, but L.A. will try to keep him working on his typical rest unless the situation necessitates it.
Snell showed some rust when he started NLDS Game 2, which was just his third appearance in the span of 2 1/2 weeks because of left groin tightness that flared up in mid-September. He would be working on extended rest if the Dodgers push him to Game 3, but having some more time to fine-tune his delivery might be helpful given how little he has pitched recently.
Remarkably, the Dodgers are 7-0 when Glasnow pitches in a postseason game for them. That Glasnow is the No. 4 starter in this rotation speaks to the depth of the group, as he could be the ace on many other staffs around the Majors.

item.content:encoded:
The Athletic has live coverage of the MLB Playoffs, including the ALDS Game 2s of White Sox vs Guardians and Yankees vs Rays.
After three days of Wild Card Series action, the dust has settled and four teams (Houston Astros, Boston Red Sox, Philadelphia Phillies and Chicago Cubs) have found themselves on an early vacation. Major League Baseball’s 12-team postseason field has been whittled to eight.
Now, the race for the World Series shifts to the next round: the Division Series. Four teams (Cleveland Guardians, Los Angeles Dodgers, Tampa Bay Rays and Milwaukee Brewers) that had first-round byes will now be in action. Additionally, while the Wild Card Series featured a best-of-three format, the Division Series will be best-of-five.
Here’s how MLB’s bracket looks right now:
You can watch the MLB playoffs on Fubo (Stream Free Now).
What is Saturday’s MLB Playoff schedule and starters?
White Sox at Guardians (AL Division Series Game 1): Hagen Smith vs. Parker Messick
First pitch: 1 p.m. ET (TBS)
After the 23-year-old Smith pitched three scoreless innings in Game 1 of the Wild Card Series against the Astros, the White Sox turn to him for an encore performance in Game 1 of the ALDS. While the club was able to pile on six runs against the Astros in a win, it won’t be as easy against the Guardians and Messick.
An All-Star this season, Messick finished his rookie campaign with a 2.56 ERA and 193 strikeouts over 32 starts. Against the White Sox, Messick carded a 2.81 ERA in four starts (25 2/3 innings).
Braves at Dodgers (NL Division Series Game 1): TBD vs. Tarik Skubal
First pitch: 4 p.m. ET (Fox)
Having burned Chris Sale to take Thursday’s winner-take-all game against the Phillies, and with Tyler Mahle also unavailable, the Braves appear to be looking at another bullpen game.
“They’ve pitched in big situations during the season, and no matter who we really see right now in that bullpen in any situation, no matter what inning it is, we’re feeling pretty confident about them,” catcher Drake Baldwin told reporters.
The Dodgers, coming off a first-round bye, will counter with Tarik Skubal, the crown jewel acquisition of this year’s trade deadline. The AL’s reigning Cy Young Award winner has a 2.61 ERA with his new team, his final starts before reaching a highly anticipated free agency.
Yankees at Rays (AL Division Series Game 1): Gerrit Cole vs. Drew Rasmussen
First pitch: 6:30 p.m. ET (TBS)
Faced with an embarrassment of riches on the pitching side, the Yankees will deploy 2023 AL Cy Young Award winner Gerrit Cole against the AL East champs. After Cole in Game 1, the Yankees will have Cam Schlittler in Game 2 and some variation of Max Fried or Carlos Rodón in Games 3 and 4, the last matchup only if necessary.
On the Tampa Bay side, Drew Rasmussen, arguably one of the most underrated aces in the sport, will get the ball at Tropicana Field. For his career, Rasmussen has a 1.81 ERA in 11 games (10 starts) against the Yankees.
Padres at Brewers (NL Division Series Game 1): Robbie Ray vs. Jacob Misiorowski
First pitch: 8:30 p.m. ET (FS1)
Saturday’s final matchup will feature two pitchers at opposite ends of their careers. On the San Diego side, Robbie Ray, the 2021 AL Cy Young Award winner, has been largely unable to replicate the success he had that season. After a deadline trade from the San Francisco Giants to the Padres, Ray has carded a 5.02 ERA over nine starts.
For the Brewers, Jacob Misiorowski is just getting started. An All-Star in his rookie year, Misiorowski finished his sophomore campaign as the favorite to win the NL Cy Young Award, leading MLB with a 1.80 ERA and 252 strikeouts. He’s wowed the sport with his ability to repeatedly fire fastballs in excess of 100 mph, and there’s reason to believe that, at 24 years old, his best is yet to come.
What to know about each Division Series matchup
White Sox at Guardians: The two AL Central clubs played each other 13 times during the regular season, with the White Sox winning the season series 7-6. That, however, was not enough to overcome a late surge by the Guardians and a collapse by Chicago that led to the White Sox losing control of the division and having to play their way out of the wild card.
Now, the two clubs will meet again for at least three games, a spot in the Championship Series on the line. By winning the division and finishing with a better record than the AL West winner, the Guardians were granted a first-round bye. No mind, the White Sox dispatched the Astros in two games and have been off since Thursday. That extra rest has allowed the club to realign its depleted pitching staff.
One thing to watch: How Chicago’s thin, matchup-dependent pitching staff is deployed against Cleveland’s newfound offense — the club led the AL in wRC+ (108) from Aug. 1 onward. The urgency, or lack thereof, by White Sox manager Will Venable could swing the series either direction.
Braves at Dodgers: The Braves’ pitching staff will enter Game 1 with very little margin for error, as it will likely be a group effort without a starter available. That alone could be the difference, as teams that take Game 1 in any best-of-five series have historically won the series 72 percent of the time. That said, these Dodgers have not played their best against the Braves, losing the season series 5-1, including a late-August sweep when Tyler Glasnow and Yoshinobu Yamamoto both pitched.
One thing to watch: Shohei Ohtani’s ability to contribute. The four-time MVP has spent much of the second half of the season compromised, leading to an abbreviated September, with some of it on the injured list.
“I do feel like my swing is in a better place, feels smooth, and just a little tweaks here and there, and I’ll be ready for tomorrow,” Ohtani said through interpreter Will Ireton.
Yankees at Rays: Only one team had a better record over its final 30 games than the Rays, who went 20-10 to fend off a late Yankees push to claim the AL East. That, plus a 55-26 home record that tied the Brewers for the best in MLB, has Tampa Bay inching toward its first World Series appearance since 2020. To get there, the Rays will need to beat the Yankees, who made quick work of the Red Sox in the wild-card round. That they did so without Aaron Judge on the roster or needing to call on Giancarlo Stanton in a pinch hit capacity is all the more impressive.
One thing to watch: Junior Caminero was 20 years old the last time the Rays made the postseason, going hitless in two at-bats. Since then, Caminero, now 23, has morphed into a perennial All-Star, hitting 40 home runs in consecutive seasons, the latter of which should earn him major MVP consideration. Few players love the big stage as much as Caminero. One of those players just so happens to be Cam Schlittler, the presumptive AL Cy Young Award winner, who will take the ball at least once this series. How these two match up will be one of the best subplots of this postseason.
Padres at Brewers: In a battle between arguably MLB’s hottest team (the Padres) and the league’s best team all season (the Brewers), there will be a lot of firsts. This is San Diego’s first Division Series under new owners José E. Feliciano and his wife and business partner Kwanza Jones. It will be the first extended runway for Padres rookie catcher Ethan Salas. It will be the first postseason series for Christian Yelich as the Brewers’ captain. And it will be the first time Misiorowski faces these Padres since May.
Should Milwaukee win, it will be the first time in franchise history that the club has made it to back-to-back league championship series. If San Diego upsets MLB’s No. 1 team, it will be the club’s first trip since 2022 and just its fourth overall.
One thing to watch: The bullpens. Behind multiple high-leverage arms, San Diego has made the late innings nearly impossible for opposing teams. If there’s one club that can match the Padres in that regard, it’s the Brewers. The late innings will likely be the deciding factor in who advances.

ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. – How the Yankees' Bay State duo of Cam Schlittler and Ben Rice performed in the Wild Card Series against the Red Sox – drafted out of Massachusetts – was also a take-a-bow moment for player development.
"Just impressive to see these young guys step into the biggest stage at the biggest moment,'' said Yankees captain Aaron Judge, their supreme first-round pick (32nd overall) from the 2013 draft.
Here's a look at the other Yankees drafted and developed players who could impact the best-of-five Division Series against the AL champion Tampa Bay Rays:
George Lombard Jr.
Age: 21
Yankees draft info: 1st round (26th overall) in 2023.
In his first taste of postseason – with 42 games of MLB experience – the shortstop handled his position well and went 4-for-8 at the plate.
"A couple of years ago, he was playing high school baseball,'' Judge said of Lombard, while praising the Yanks' rookie and sophomore class in general.
"Just a really good player,'' Max Fried said of Lombard Jr. "He's got a slow heartbeat.''
Spencer Jones
Age: 25
Yankees draft info: 1st round (25th overall) in 2022.
Despite Trent Grisham's return, Jones – who batted .389/1.107 OPS in 59 MLB plate appearances vs. lefties – started in center field against Payton Tolle in the Wild Card opener.
The lefty-hitting Jones was shifted to right field vs. Sonny Gray in Game 2, batting cleanup, with Grisham in center.
Jones went 2-for-8 with a walk and four strikeouts in the ALWC.
Judge's status could impact his late game at-bats, if the captain is on the roster, but the 6-foot-7 slugger has earned his opportunity as a regular in postseason.
Ben Rice
Age: 27
Yankees draft info: 12th round in 2021.
Rice destroyed the Red Sox in the Yanks' 9-0, Wild Card Series Game 1 win, with two homers - including a grand slam - among his four hits, with six RBI as the DH.
With 41 homers this year, Rice joined Judge as the only drafted Yankees to reach the 40-homer mark in a single regular season.
Expect Rice to continue batting leadoff against the Rays' right-handed starters. Also, he's a .458 hitter with five homers and a 1.685 OPS in seven career games at the Trop.
Anthony Volpe
Age: 25
Yankees draft info: 1st round (30th overall) in 2019.
Volpe started the Wild Card opener vs. the lefty Tolle, going 1-for-3 at second base, a new MLB position for him upon his return; he was optioned to Triple-A with Lombard's early August call-up.
Lefty-hitting Jazz Chisholm Jr., on the bench in WC Game 1, started Game 2 vs. the right-handed Gray and went 2-for-3 with a walk in a clinching 9-2 victory.
Given the Rays' right-handed rotation, Volpe might be a bench player this series, utilized later in games for his infield versatility (including some third base) and as a pinch-runner.
Cam Schlittler
Age: 25
Yankees draft info: 7th round in 2022.
Red Sox Nation has already seen enough postseason Schlittler, helping take Boston out of the last two AL Wild Card Series.
After his 117-pitch scoreless effort in Tuesday's Wild Card opener, Schlittler gets the ball in Monday's ALDS Game 2, on one extra day of rest.
That also puts him in line for a possible Game 5 on normal rest. Both games are at Trop, and Schlittler owns a 1.16 ERA in 17 road starts this year.
Will Warren
Age: 27
Yankees draft info: 8th round in 2021.
Moved into a multi-inning relief role in postseason, Warren tossed 1.2 innings (one run) following Fried in Game 2.
He should fit that same role against the Rays, with the ability to take over for a shaky or injured starter, or to provide a bridge to the high-leverage duo of Paul Blackburn and Brent Headrick, leading into David Bednar.
Austin Wells
Age: 27
Yankees draft info: 1st round (28th overall) in 2020.
At the plate, the lefty-hitting Wells picked it up considerably after a brutal first four months, but his value behind the plate - and his knack for ABS challenges - has been a constant.
As for defending the speedy, daring Rays, "they love to run and take advantage,'' said Wells, emphasizing the limiting of walks in this series.
Wells has been paired all year with Game 1 starter Gerrit Cole, who praised the "role Austin has played in run prevention'' for a staff that led the league in ERA.

Cubs' Pete Crow-Armstrong makes honest admission about struggles in NL Wild Card against Padres originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
It was a disappointing Wild Card series for the Chicago Cubs against the San Diego Padres, to say the least, and they were eventually swept.
The Cubs were unable to do anything on either side of the baseball for the better part of this series, with the offense being the biggest issue.
Chicago entered this Wild Card series with a chance to make some noise in the postseason, but the offense went absolutely quiet.
Expected National League MVP Award winner Pete Crow-Armstrong struggled just as much as anybody on the Cubs roster. Crow-Armstrong went 0-for-7 with four strikeouts, walking just once in the series, putting together a stolen base after that one walk.
Speaking to reporters after the game, the Cubs' 24-year-old superstar understands that he needed to be better, and while anybody can look at any numbers they want, it was obvious that he didn't contribute.
"We were challenged this year," Crow-Armstrong said, per The Athletic. "This team showed a lot of heart and a lot of fight through all the challenges. But I would say, to start: I show up. I show up when it matters in these games. That would help us immediately. But that's all I got right now."
"You can look at the scoreboard, you can look at the stat sheet, wherever you get your numbers from, and it is clear to see that I didn't contribute," Crow-Armstrong said.
Crow-Armstrong has never been the type of guy to beat around the bush and say he didn't do what was needed on both sides of the ball.
Unfortunately for the young man, this was a very disappointing series, one that he's going to have to live with throughout the remainder of the offseason. He had an incredible regular season, finishing the campaign with 45 home runs and a .943 OPS.
That wasn't even close to what he was able to do in the postseason.
